Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi describe the camels as left unattended because their owners have no thought for them. Ibn 'Ashur understands it as one of the cosmic signs preceding the resurrection.

Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy, take the word to mean pregnant camels. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya also record the view that the ishar are clouds left without rain, and others take them to be fields left unplanted or homes left empty. Abu Hayyan mentions that Ibn Kathir is said to read the verb with a doubled consonant, while a lighter reading attributed to Mudar was judged by some scholars to be an error, though Ibn Khalawayh and others accept it as a dialect form.

This verse, which opens the list of signs of the Day of Judgment in the surah, speaks of the wild beasts being gathered. The commentators differ on the meaning of the word hashr. Ibn 'Abbas, followed by 'Ikrima, takes it to mean that they die, since every creature dies except jinn and humans, who will be made to stand on the Day of Resurrection. Ubayy ibn Ka'b understands it as being mixed together, the beasts mingling with people in panic. Al-Tabari, whose view Ibn Kathir supports, prefers the sense of being gathered, citing the verse about birds being gathered. Qatada and others say that every creature will be gathered, even flies, so that justice is done among them: the hornless animal will be avenged against the horned one, and then told to become dust. Al-Razi reports that the Mu'tazilites see this as God compensating animals for their suffering in this world, while the Ash'aris see no obligation upon God. Al-Suyuti and others simply say that they will be gathered after resurrection for judgment. The common ground is a general assembly of animals, though the manner of it remains debated.

This passage of Surah At-Takwir describes the terrors of the Day of Judgment and the signs that precede it. The verse "And when the seas are set ablaze" is understood by the commentators in several ways. Most of them say the seas will be filled and burst forth until they become one sea, or else they will be kindled and become a blazing fire. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil add that fresh water will mix with salt water until all the seas become one sea, while al-Hasan and Qatada hold that the water will dry up so that not a drop remains. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Ubayy ibn Ka'b say they will be set on fire and become a blaze; Ibn Kathir cites a report in which the jinn tell mankind that they found the sea ablaze.

On the reading, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the word without doubling the letter, while the others read it with doubling. Ibn Jarir judges the two readings close in meaning and both correct. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir favour the sense of filling, which is the most common. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the term refers to the overflowing of the seas and the mixing of their waters, a result of the disruption of atmospheric pressure. Some commentators read the verse symbolically, but Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan reject this, Abu Hayyan stating that the Qur'an is in clear Arabic with no hidden symbols.

As for "And when the souls are paired", the best-known view among the early scholars is that each soul will be joined to its like: the righteous with the righteous in Paradise, the wicked with the wicked in Hell, as reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir consider this the most sound. 'Ikrima and al-Sha'bi say that the souls will be returned to the bodies.

This verse from Surah At-Takwir describes one of the events of the Day of Judgment: the pairing of souls, meaning that each soul is joined to its counterparts. The commentators differ on what "pairing" means. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, as transmitted through an-Nu'man ibn Bashir, and Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Kathir understood it as each person being grouped with those of his kind: the righteous with the righteous in Paradise, the wicked with the wicked in Hell, and Jews with Jews and Christians with Christians. Rabi' ibn Khuthaym said a man will be gathered with the one whose deeds he followed. Al-Tabari judged this to be the most sound interpretation, citing the verses about the three groups of people and the command to gather the wrongdoers together with their companions.

Other views are also reported. Ash-Sha'bi, 'Ikrima and ad-Dahhak take it to mean the return of the spirits into the bodies. Muqatil and 'Ata' say the souls of believers will be paired with the wide-eyed houris and those of disbelievers with devils. Others say souls are joined to their deeds. Ibn al-Qayyim regarded the first meaning as the most evident.

This event belongs to the signs that precede the reckoning, after which the records of deeds are unfolded and each soul knows what good or evil it has done.

This passage of Surat at-Takwir describes the terrors of the Day of Resurrection: the sun is folded up, the stars fall and scatter, the mountains are set in motion, the pregnant she-camels are neglected, the wild beasts are gathered, the seas are set ablaze, souls are paired, the buried infant girl is questioned, the scrolls of deeds are unrolled, the sky is stripped away, Hell is kindled and Paradise brought near; the answer to all these conditions is "every soul will know what it has brought forth". The commentators give closely related meanings. On the word takwir, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress gathering and folding, Ibn 'Abbas speaks of the light vanishing, Mujahid of its dissolution, and al-Zamakhshari of the light being rolled up. On the beasts, Ibn 'Abbas takes their gathering to mean their death, Ubayy ibn Ka'b their mingling, and Qatada their assembly for retaliation. On the seas being kindled, some take it as their filling, others as their ignition, and al-Hasan as their drying up. The mawudah is the girl buried alive in pre-Islamic times, and her questioning serves to rebuke her killer; some read the verb as sa'alat, meaning she lodges a complaint. On the pairing of souls, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the sense of like joined with like in good and evil, relying on a report from 'Umar, while others take it as the return of souls to bodies, the view of 'Ikrima and al-Sha'bi. The commentators agree that the scrolls are the records of deeds, that the sky is folded or torn away, that Hell is kindled, and that Paradise is brought near.

This verse belongs to a sequence of signs of the Last Day. It describes the buried infant girl, the mawudah, who will be asked for what sin she was killed. The commentators explain that the question serves to rebuke her killer, since she had done no wrong. Killing daughters was practised out of fear of shame or of poverty, and some Arabs carried it out cruelly, digging a pit in the desert or having the mother give birth over a hole. Ibn Abbas and others report that she will answer that she was killed without sin. Al-Zamakhshari uses the verse to argue that the children of polytheists are not punished, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report other views. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the question is meant to terrify the killer. The readings differ: most read qutilat, Abu Ja'far reads it with a doubled letter, and Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas read sa'alat, meaning she made a claim. Al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi relate that al-Farazdaq praised his grandfather Sa'sa'a ibn Najiya, who ransomed many girls destined for burial, and that Islam ended the custom. Ibn Kathir cites Qays ibn 'Asim, whom the Prophet told to free a slave or sacrifice a camel for each daughter he had buried.

This verse, the tenth of Surat al-Takwir, belongs to the scenes of the Day of Judgment with which the sura opens. The commentators explain that the pages are the registers of human deeds, good and bad. Qatada says that a person's register is dictated to him, folded up at death, and then unfolded on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi likewise hold that it is folded by death and spread out on the Last Day, so that each person stands before his own record and learns what is in it. The readers differed over how the word "spread" should be read, and al-Tabari judged both readings sound, the intensive form suiting the plural noun in the verse about "spread-out pages". Ibn Kathir and others take the spreading to be for the reckoning. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud add that it may mean the pages are separated among their owners, some receiving theirs in the right hand and others in the left. Ibn 'Ashur explains that spreading means opening the folds so the writing can be read. Several commentators cite the hadith of Umm Salama about people being occupied by the spreading of the records, which they connect with the time of the reckoning.

Verse 11 of Surat al-Takwir describes one of the terrors of the Day of Judgment: the sky is "kushitat", meaning it is stripped away and removed from its place, as a hide is stripped from a slaughtered animal. The commentators broadly agree on this meaning. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba explain the word as pulling off and folding up, al-Zajjaj as being torn away like a ceiling is lifted off, and Muqatil as being uncovered over those within it. Al-Tabari gives the sense of pulling, then folding, and reports from Mujahid that it means "drawn away". Ibn Mas'ud's reading "qushitat" with a qaf is noted, and the scholars say that kaf and qaf interchange in Arabic with the same meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi link this folding to the Qur'anic image of the sky rolled up like a scroll for writings. Few commentators describe the process in detail; most simply convey the immensity of that day's terror. This verse is one of twelve events introduced by "idha", whose answer is that every soul will know what it has brought forward.

This verse describes one of the terrors of the Day of Judgement: when Hellfire is kindled, and Paradise is brought near to the righteous, then every soul will know what it has brought forward, whether good or evil. Most commentators explain the verb 'su'irat' as 'was lit and set ablaze.' Qatada, quoted by al-Tabari, says that it is kindled by God's wrath and the sins of the children of Adam. The reciters of Medina, Syria and Hafs from 'Asim read the doubled form, meaning it is kindled again and again, while the others read the single form. Al-Tabari considers both readings correct and does not choose between them. Regarding Paradise, al-Hasan says its people will be brought near to it without it moving from its place, while Ibn Zayd understands it to mean that Paradise is adorned. Al-Tabari and most others keep the sense of drawing near, since the root conveys nearness. The answer to the conditional clauses is 'every soul will know what it has brought forward.' Ibn 'Abbas counts twelve signs at the start of the sūra, six in this world and six in the next, all linked to this single answer. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the singular 'soul' is used for emphasis, a common Arabic way of speaking of the whole category, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees the singular as highlighting the individual's insignificance and lack of means to defend himself.

The commentators explain that the verse "And when Paradise is brought near" means that Paradise will be drought close to the God-fearing on the Day of Resurrection. It is one of the twelve events listed at the start of the surah, all of which share the single answer "a soul will know what it has presented." The commentators agree that these scenes belong to the Day of Judgment, with Paradise brought near to believers just as the Fire is kindled for disbelievers.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take "uzlifat" to mean "brought near." Al-Hasan al-Basri adds that the righteous are the ones who draw near to it, without Paradise leaving its place, while Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd suggests the meaning "adorned." Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi regard the first meaning as preferable, since the root "zulfa" denotes nearness in Arabic. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari also link the verse to the parallel statement that Paradise is brought near to the pious, and Ibn Kathir sees its mention as the counterpart to the kindling of the Fire.

Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that "soul" appears in the singular with a general sense, the singular emphasising the weakness of the individual before the event. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the answer covers all twelve events, six occurring in the present life and six in the hereafter.

The commentators explain that this verse is the answer to twelve conditional clauses introduced by “idha”, which describe the events of the Last Day and the signs that precede it: the folding up of the sun and the loss of its light, the falling of the stars, the moving of the mountains, the abandoning of pregnant camels, the gathering of the wild beasts, the kindling of the seas, the pairing of souls with their like, the questioning of the buried girl about the crime committed against her, the spreading of the scrolls of deeds, the stripping away of the sky, the kindling of the Blaze, and the bringing near of Paradise. The meaning of the verse is that at that time every soul knows what it has sent forward of good or evil.

The commentators agree that the passage affirms the resurrection and recompense, that “soul” here refers to every soul though it is singular and indefinite, and that “knew” is the answer to all the conditions. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, as reported by Ibn Kathir, said on reaching this verse: “this is what the discourse was leading to”. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the indefinite is used for exaggeration in the manner of inverted speech, while al-Alusi and Abu al-Suʿud take it to affirm that each individual will know.

Opinions differ on the meaning of “what it has brought forth”. Most take it to mean the deeds themselves or their records, and some, including Abu al-Suʿud and al-Alusi, hold that deeds take on forms in the hereafter according to their nature. Views also differ on the pairing of souls: ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas understood it as each person being joined with his like, ʿIkrima as the return of souls to bodies, and ʿAtaʾ as the believers being joined with the houris and the disbelievers with devils. On the buried girl, most see her questioning as a rebuke to her killer, while Zamakhshari draws from it an argument about the fate of the children of polytheists, which Ibn Kathir does not accept as decisive.

In this verse God swears by the al-Khunnas, stars that recede in their course and disappear from view. The commentators give several interpretations. Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan and Qatada take them to be the stars in general, which hide by day and appear by night. Ali, Ibn Zayd and al-Farra' identify them with the five wandering planets, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, whose apparent motion turns back. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i and Jabir ibn Zayd understand them as wild cattle, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say they are gazelles. Al-Tabari concludes that the verse may cover anything that recedes, then hides and returns. On the verb 'as'asa, most say the night has turned away, al-Hasan says it has drawn near, and al-Mubarrad holds that the word covers both senses. The oath is answered by the statement that the Quran is the word of a noble messenger. Most exegetes take this messenger to be Gabriel, while others say he is the Prophet. Gabriel is described as strong, esteemed near the Lord of the Throne, obeyed among the angels and trustworthy. The commentators reject the charge of madness against the Prophet and deny that the Quran is the speech of a devil. Readers differ on the word bi-dannin: with the letter dad it means stingy, with the letter zay it means accused. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu 'Ubayd prefer the second reading, while others prefer the first.

God swears by the stars that recede and hide, that run their course and then withdraw into their lairs, by the night as it draws near or turns away, and by the dawn as its light spreads. The sworn matter is that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger, whom most commentators identify as Gabriel: he is strong, held in high rank with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed in the heavens, and trusted with the revelation. On the meaning of 'al-khunnas' and 'al-jawari al-kunnas' the scholars differ widely. Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take them to be the stars, and most of them specify the five wandering planets, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak take them to be gazelles, while Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i and Jabir ibn Zayd take them to be wild cattle. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Tabari favour the first view, since it fits the mention of night and dawn that follows. The commentators agree that 'as'asa' can mean both the approach and the retreat of night, and that 'tanaffasa' describes the spreading of morning light. As for the 'noble messenger', most identify him as Gabriel, though some say it is the Prophet. On the word 'dannin', the readings differ between the letter dad, meaning miserly, and dha, meaning accused; both are accepted, and Ibn Kathir treats both as transmitted. All the commentators reject the idea that the Qur'an is the speech of a devil or that the Prophet was mad.

God swears by the stars that recede, that run their course and then hide, by the night as it draws in or withdraws, and by the dawn as it breathes out its light. The answer to the oath is that the Quran is the word of a noble messenger, which most commentators identify as Gabriel, who conveys it from God. He is strong, held in high rank near the Lord of the Throne, obeyed in the heavens and trusted with the revelation. On the stars called al-khunnas, Ali and Ibn Abbas, along with most exegetes, understand the wandering planets, Ali and Ibn Abbas naming five of them, while Hasan and Qatada take it to mean all the stars. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Kathir report other readings: wild cattle according to Ibn Mas'ud, and gazelles according to Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The verb 'as'asa is recognised by the lexicographers as a word with two opposite meanings: Ali, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd take it to mean that the night withdrew, while Hasan takes it to mean that it advanced with its darkness. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri prefer the advancing sense, while al-Shinqiti and others prefer withdrawal. As for the word dannin, most read it with the letter dad, meaning miserly, while Ibn Kathir, Abu Ubayd and others read it with the letter zay, meaning accused. Finally, the verse about whoever among you wishes to go straight shows, according to the commentators, that human will is fulfilled only by God's will, which refutes both the doctrine of absolute freedom and that of compulsion.

In these verses God swears by the stars that recede, vanish and hide, by the night as it draws in or withdraws, and by the dawn when its light spreads and becomes clear day, that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger. Commentators have debated who this messenger is. The majority, including al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identify him as Gabriel, describing his strength, his high rank with the Lord of the Throne, his obeyed status among the angels and his trustworthiness. As for the dawn that "breathes", al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi explain it as the appearance and rising of light, while others take it as the spreading of the day; al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy read it as a metaphor, the breeze that accompanies dawn being like a breath.

The commentators agree that these verses answer the pagans who accused the Prophet ﷺ of madness or soothsaying, and that the Qur'an is not the word of a devil. They differ on the "receding stars": 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and others take them to be the stars or the five wandering planets, while Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak cite wild cattle or gazelles; Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim prefer the stars, since night and dawn are mentioned next. The verb 'assa'asa is read by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada as "it departed", by al-Hasan as "it approached", and al-Mubarrad sees a word with two opposite meanings.

On the reading "bi-dannin" (with the dad) or "bi-zannin" (with the zay), the exegetes give respectively "stingy" and "suspected". Ibn Kathir considers both readings sound and compatible in meaning. Finally, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Juzayy connect the verse "for whoever among you wills to go straight" with divine will: human choice takes effect only if God wills it, rejecting both the fatalists and the Qadarites.

God swears by the stars that recede and hide, that run and then withdraw, by the night when it draws near or retreats, and by the dawn when its light spreads, that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger. Most commentators, following Ibn Abbas and Qatada, understand this as Gabriel, who brought it down: he is mighty, held in high rank with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed in the heavens and trustworthy with the revelation. Al-Mawardi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya note the possibility that the messenger is Muhammad, a view attributed to Ibn 'Isa and others, though it is not the dominant one. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir consider the qualities described to fit the angelic messenger. On the khunnas and kunnas, Ali, Qatada and Ibn Kathir say they are the stars, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibrahim say wild oxen, and Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr say gazelles; al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur largely take them as the planets. On 'as'asa, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it as the night receding, while al-Hasan takes it as its approach, and Ibn Kathir favours approach. On the reading with dad (miserly) or za (accused), the readers differ; Abu 'Ubayd preferred za, since the Quraysh accused the Prophet of falsehood rather than of withholding. The commentators do not settle between these readings.

This verse describes the messenger of the Qur'an, whom the great majority of commentators identify as the angel Jibril. He is praised for his strength, for his high standing with the Lord of the Throne, and for being obeyed among the angels. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take strength literally, recalling the report that he lifted the cities of Lot's people on his wing and overturned them. Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud add that it may also mean firmness in carrying out God's command without any shortfall, a moral sense that Ibn al-Qayyim develops.

Almost all agree that the phrase with the Lord of the Throne expresses honour and closeness rather than a physical location, as al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain. Al-Razi, citing al-Kisa'i, understands makin as one who has standing and influence, whose requests are granted. On what the phrase modifies, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy report two views, one attaching it to strength and the other to makin, and Ibn Juzayy prefers the second. Abu Hayyan records a reading with a damma on the thaa, which makes it a conjunction, while al-Zamakhshari explains the adverb thamma as stressing the trust placed in him. Finally, Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes the noble messenger of Surat al-Haqqah, whom he takes to be the Prophet, from the one in this verse, who is Jibril.

In these opening verses, God swears by the stars that recede, withdraw and hide, by the night as it draws near or retreats, and by the dawn as its light spreads, that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identify this messenger as Gabriel, and describe him as strong, highly honoured with God, obeyed among the angels, and trustworthy with the revelation. The meaning of 'the receding, hidden stars' is disputed. 'Ali, Qatada and al-Hasan take it to mean the stars in general, or the five planets according to 'Ali, while Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Jabir ibn Zayd take it to mean wild cattle and gazelles. Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qasimi prefer the astral reading, since it fits the mention of night and dawn that follows. The verb 'as'asa is also debated: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada read it as 'withdrew', al-Hasan as 'drew near', and some combine both senses. The passage then states that Muhammad is not mad, that he saw Gabriel on the bright horizon, and that he is not suspect concerning the unseen. Most read the word as dan (he is not stingy), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Juzayy favour reading it as zan (he is not accused). The passage ends by rebuking the disbelievers, stating that the Qur'an is a reminder to all worlds, and affirming that human willing succeeds only by God's will, a point many link to a circumstance of revelation involving Abu Jahl.

The commentators explain that this verse denies the accusation of madness that the Meccan disbelievers hurled at the Prophet ﷺ, and that it forms part of the answer to the oath opening the sura. The word "companion" refers to the Prophet ﷺ, whom the Meccans had known closely for years. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take the companion to be Muhammad ﷺ, while al-Zamakhshari reads the surrounding verses as showing the superiority of Gabriel over the Prophet, an opinion that al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur reject, arguing that the context only aims to clear the Prophet of the charge of madness. The verse is linked to the vision at the clear horizon: according to Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Abbas, the Prophet ﷺ saw Gabriel in his true form on the eastern horizon, and Ibn Kathir specifies that this was the first vision, the one at Hira. The claim that the Qur'an is the speech of a satan is rejected by all: Ibn Kathir notes that devils can neither carry it nor desire it. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy report that the Meccans claimed a demon dictated it to him. Commentators stress that the Prophet's known reason and integrity make such a charge untenable.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a great oath by the stars, the night and the dawn, affirming that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger, Gabriel. It then denies that the Prophet ﷺ is mad and states that he saw Gabriel in his true form on the clear horizon. For most scholars, the "clear horizon" is the place where the sun rises in the east, as Qatada and Mujahid say, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi follow this reading; a report from Mujahid specifies the area of Ajyad, east of Mecca, and others take it to mean the horizon of the sky in general. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that this vision is the first, after the revelation in the cave of Hira, while the vision at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary is mentioned in Surat an-Najm. On the reading, most readers of Medina and Kufa read "dannin" with the letter dad, meaning he is not stingy with teaching, while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "zannin" with the letter za, meaning he is not suspected. At-Tabari prefers the dad reading because it matches the mushaf script, while Abu 'Ubayd prefers the za reading since the disbelievers accused him rather than being stingy with him. The following verses deny that the Qur'an is the word of an accursed devil, rebuke the listeners for their going astray, and state, as Ibn Kathir and at-Tabari explain, that the Qur'an is a reminder to the worlds for whoever wishes to go straight, while human will remains subject to God's will, a statement linked in the occasion of revelation reports to Abu Jahl.

This verse affirms that the Prophet ﷺ is neither accused falsely nor stingy in conveying the revelation and the news of the unseen, and that the Qur'an is not the word of an accursed devil, as the Quraysh claimed. The commentators explain that the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and that "al-ghayb" means the revelation, the news of the heavens, and whatever is hidden from people. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the reading with the letter dad, which appears in the mushafs, means he is not stingy, withholding nothing of what he was taught. Al-Tabari also reports that some grammarians understood it as "weak", a view the others do not adopt. The reading with the letter zay, "zanin", means "suspected": Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it this way, and most exegetes take it as "falsely accused". Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, since the unbelievers did not accuse the Prophet of stinginess but of lying. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi record both readings and their arguments. The commentators agree that the verse denies the Qur'an is the speech of a devil, which the Quraysh claimed by saying a devil dictated it through the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that the two letters must be distinguished in recitation. On "where are you going", Qatada takes it to mean turning away from the Book, while al-Zajjaj takes it as seeking a clearer path than the Qur'an. Finally, rightness depends on God's will, as Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di observe. Ibn 'Ashur regards both readings as equally authentic, without choosing between them.

The commentators agree that this verse denies that the Qur'an is the speech of an accursed devil who eavesdrops on the heavens. Its message is not of the kind delivered by soothsayers, who get their news from the jinn, but is God's own word and revelation. Most of the exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, connect the verse to the charge by the Quraysh that the Prophet ﷺ was a soothsayer, and to their claim that a devil was dictating the Qur'an to him; al-Kalbi adds that the Qur'an is neither poetry nor divination. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the Qur'an does not come from those who steal hearing from heaven, nor from the revelations they pass to their human allies among the diviners. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy stress that devils can neither carry this message nor want to. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a return to the subject of the Qur'an's truthfulness after a long digression about the angel and the Prophet, and as linked to the mention of the unseen in the previous verse. The verse ends with a rebuke in the form of a question, 'Where then are you going?' Qatada reads it as asking why people turn away from God's Book, while al-Zajjaj reads it as asking what clearer path they could take than the one already made plain to them.

This verse closes the rhetorical question of reproach in the surah. The commentators explain its meaning as: where are you going, turning away from this Qur'an and from obedience to God? Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud read it as a way of misleading them, likened to someone who has left the clear road and is asked where he is going. Al-Zajjaj paraphrases it as: what path could you follow that is clearer than the one that has been made plain to you? Qatada says: where do you turn away from My Book and My obedience? Ibn Kathir understands it as a reproach to minds that go astray in denying this manifest Qur'an. Al-Tabari, citing the grammarians, notes that the Arabs say 'I went to Syria' without a preposition, and he cites a line of verse where the same usage appears. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree on the general sense. The scholars agree that the question is one of reproach and a statement of fact, coming after the affirmation that the Qur'an is a reminder to the worlds. Ibn 'Ashur observes that it is a parenthetical clause linked by fa to the preceding proofs, and that it may also express the inability of the opponents to find any other way. Al-Jaza'iri takes it as a reminder of the clear path. Al-Qasimi adds that the Qur'an's proof is complete, so any path away from it leads to error, and Ibn Sa'di connects it with the reminder for those who wish to go straight.

The commentators explain that the verse means the Qur'an is only a reminder and admonition to all the worlds, meaning humans and jinn. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, benefiting from it belongs only to whoever wishes to keep to the truth and remain steadfast in faith. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari, take the phrase "for whoever among you wills to go straight" as an apposition to "for all the worlds". Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya relay the report that Abu Jahl, upon hearing this, said the choice was theirs; the following verse answered that human willing happens only by God's will. Al-Zamakhshari reads this will as divine support, and reports the Mu'tazili view that a person's acts are created by himself, while his gloss sets against it the Sunni position of divine creation with human acquisition. For "where then are you going?", al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a call to return to the right path, like one who leaves the road, whereas Ibn Kathir reads it as a rebuke for rejecting the Qur'an. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse warns against judging the religion by the conduct of some Muslims. Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn Sa'di stress that human choice is real, while affirming that it is subordinate to God's will, on whose support success depends.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage stating that the Qur'an is a reminder and admonition for all humanity, and that only the one who wants to follow the straight path benefits from it. Mujahid defines steadfastness (istiqama) as following the truth, and al-Tabari reads the verse as meaning that the Qur'an is a reminder only for whoever among you wishes to take the right path, believe in it and act upon it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that "for whoever among you wills" is an apposition to "the worlds": those who choose to be upright by entering Islam are the ones who truly benefit from the reminder, even though the address is to everyone.

As for the words "and you will not will except that God wills", the commentators agree that human will takes effect only when God wills it. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that this was revealed in response to Abu Jahl, who said that the matter was up to them: if they wished they would be upright, and if not, they would not. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi see in the verse a refutation of the Mu'tazilites, who restrict this divine will to compulsion; al-Zamakhshari reads it as divine guidance and favour. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that human beings have a genuine will, so no one can use predestination as an excuse for neglect.

The commentators explain that this verse completes the one before it: the Quran is a reminder for all the worlds, but the one who benefits from it is whoever wills to walk upright. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir clarify that uprightness means following the truth and holding firmly to it. The verse then states that human willing takes effect only through God's will, the Lord of the worlds. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir understand this divine will as God's support and guidance toward uprightness. Several sources, including al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir, report that the verse was revealed in response to Abu Jahl, who said that the matter is up to us: if we wish we will be upright, and if we wish we will not.

The scholars agree that a person has genuine choice in his actions, but that this choice depends on God's will. Al-Razi argues that willing itself requires a prior divine willing, and he judges the Mu'tazili reading, which limits the verse to compulsion, to be weak. Al-Zamakhshari reads the divine will as help and grace. Ibn 'Ashur observes that scholars differed on how to understand this divine favour: some leaned toward compulsion, others toward the servant's acquisition (kasb).

Ibn 'Uthaymin concludes that a person acts by his own will, but that this will always follows God's will, since otherwise sending messengers would carry no weight as proof.
